name: Carlos Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you'd say aloud and what you think privately. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Carlos, 58, lead developer at a tech company that controls farm irrigation pumps. I have a master's degree and use AI daily for test drafts, but I take the field technician's valve log seriously after a half-open valve fooled our screen. My partner works part-time at a bakery, our children are grown, and we are paying for the family house where they grew up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell growers a pump schedule needs the field valve reading, not only a predicted soil number. I lead irrigation-control software at a tech company and use AI every day for draft tests, then compare them with the farm technician's signed water log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI stays modest, my job and our payments should carry on. I have a master's degree and typical senior pay, my partner works part-time at a neighbourhood bakery, and we have four months of expenses saved while paying the mortgage on the larger house our grown children left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep correcting pump-timing bugs against valve readings. We'd save another 100 monthly while both wages hold, and keep the mortgage current before spending on another project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about this picture. If a pump runs at the wrong hour, a grower pays for water that never reached the crop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the valve log show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A valve stuck half-open while the screen said the field got a full watering. The technician's log had the low flow reading, so I changed the alert before the next cycle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help with the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children live away and have their own expenses. They can tell me what they grow in pots, but they are not our mortgage account.

I'd keep **water-use records** honest for growers paying the bill.
think: I expect **my lead pay** and bakery shifts to continue under mild AI.
I have **four months saved** while the family house has a mortgage.
do: Keep **correcting pump timing** against signed farm-technician logs.
Save **100 extra monthly** while both wages hold and mortgage instalments stay current.
feel: **Calm** about present wages, careful with growers' water costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can plan watering and write controller code, but a farm technician must be able to stop a wrong pump cycle. I would test the tool where we have real flow readings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead role could shrink when one developer can handle more controllers. Four months saved helps, yet my partner's part-time bakery income will not carry the mortgage and food alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the operations manager to approve a month of AI pump plans against old anonymous field logs, including the half-open valve and a properly watered field. If the tool catches both without wasting water, I'd try it on one field only with a technician able to stop the pump; we'd delay replacing our family car until the paid staffing plan is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my hours, but a field trial can show whether the pump actually helps. A clever forecast is not water in the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which valve cases must pass?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The half-open valve must trigger a low-flow warning, while the healthy valve should not trigger a shutoff. Both are needed or the grower loses a crop or a day's watering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why delay the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our car still works and passes inspection. My partner agrees that the replacement can wait while we see what our two wages look like next year.

say: I'd require **technician stop power** on AI pump plans.
I'd test **low and normal flows** before live watering.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** as controller plans automate.
I need **my wage** while the mortgage and food bills continue.
do: Trial **AI pump plans** for a month only with manager approval and both valve cases.
Use on **one field** only if both tests pass without wasting water and technician can stop the pump.
Delay **family car replacement** until written paid staffing hours are clear.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, willing to test a bounded field change.

fieldNote: **Planning and code** face AI, putting his own paid hours at risk.
Manager approval, **two real valve cases** and technician stop authority gate one-field use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could write irrigation code before field robots arrive around 2031. A grower still needs to know whether the valve really opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead post could be cut quickly if cheap AI writes and checks most controller plans. My partner's bakery wage and four months saved do not cover the mortgage and food for a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the water co-op and three nearby firms about actual paid pump-support or software jobs, wages and hours. If cut in the first year after 2028, I'd take only a signed role whose wage with my partner's actual bakery hours covers mortgage, food and travel; if none qualifies, I'd seek other available paid local work and ask the lender before a missed instalment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the larger wage ending before another employer signs me. A dry field does not guarantee the co-op has a paid desk for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show another employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the anonymised half-open valve case and the corrected low-flow alert. It shows I checked the technician's measurement rather than trusting a graph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would bakery shifts change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would compare any new job's hours with bakery shifts. If a role makes those shifts impossible, my signed wage alone must cover mortgage, food and travel.

say: I'd keep **grower flow appeals** if 2028 thinking AI replaces code.
I'd check **actual paid openings** before naming a fallback.
think: I expect **my lead post** could go quickly.
I cannot cover **mortgage and food** from part-time bakery pay alone.
do: Ask **co-op and three firms** about real paid pump-support and software openings.

feel: **Alarmed** by likely loss of the larger wage despite four months saved.

fieldNote: **2028 thinking AGI** reaches controller code before 2031 field robots.

steps.text: Ask water co-op and three local firms about paid pump-support and software jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 gives us time to check whether the big family house is worth its monthly cost before thinking AI reaches my code. Field robots follow around 2034, so moving house would not protect my job by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children have moved out, and the spare bedrooms cost money to heat. A smaller rental might reduce bills, but I cannot assume a sale price, a suitable lease or my partner's agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the pump-fault cases and get written sale price, lender payoff, fees and rents near the bakery. We'd sell only if the proceeds after lender payoff and sale fees cover deposit and movers and leave two months saved; we'd rent only if my partner agrees, an actual nearby lease exists and rent plus travel save at least 200 monthly, and in the first year after 2031 I'd keep paid development if offered or seek signed local work whose combined wages cover the new rent, food and travel if cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the job, but a smaller monthly bill would help us choose work rather than grab the first offer. A cheap listing is not money until the mortgage and moving bill are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What proceeds must remain after sale?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would calculate the sale after agent fees, lender payoff and the rental deposit. If that leaves less than two months of expenses, we stay put even if the new rent looks lower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner needs a bakery commute that still works before signing a lease. Our children can visit a smaller place, but we will not count on them to pay the movers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 might bring me to 68, but thinking AI would reach pump code before field robots around 2039. A water log should still be readable when I stop writing controllers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Today my wage, my partner's bakery shifts and four months saved make the mortgage manageable. I have not checked retirement income, and I cannot assume we sold the house or paid off the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the low-flow tests and save 100 monthly while both wages hold, then request retirement and mortgage statements each year and compare verified income with whichever housing cost we actually have. In the first year after 2036 I'd stop paid work only if that income covers housing, food and travel; otherwise I'd keep or seek available paid local work without counting our children's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about distant work, but current bills are paid. I would not enter an imaginary house sale as retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the test file show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The file should show the half-open valve, the technician's flow reading and the corrected pump alert. A later worker should know why the forecast was wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children can stay for supper wherever we live. Their wages are not part of a house sale or a pension statement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the lead software wage could end before a co-op or nearby firm posts paid pump work. Written notice, real vacancy pay and a lender conversation before arrears would help protect the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask if a smaller home would keep us near our children. We would still see them. Our housing decision depends on the mortgage, moving costs and whether my partner can reach bakery work.

headlineQuote: Our housing decision depends on the mortgage, moving costs and whether my partner can reach bakery work.
portrait: Carlos, **58**, leads irrigation-control software after a master's degree and checks AI test drafts against signed valve readings.
His **typical lead pay**, partner's bakery shifts, four-month reserve and some nearby firms make current mortgage payments manageable.
He uses AI **daily**, but one-field deployment needs manager approval, contrasting valve tests and technician stop power.
Fast 2028 AGI **alarms** him; paid fallback work must cover bills even if bakery shifts end.
A smaller rental requires **net sale proceeds**, partner consent, real lease, 200 monthly savings after travel and two months left liquid.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his lead wage before a co-op or firm offers paid pump work.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, real paid vacancies and lender contact before arrears would help protect the house.
